important, because otherwise you'll forget to do it at the times you need it most. Especially aim to
practise it whenever you get caught up in your thoughts and feelings. And as with all the other
acceptance techniques, don’t try to use this as a control strategy in order to try to feel good.
Breathing to Connect will often give rise to nice feelings such as calmness or a sense of relief. But
those are just pleasant byproducts and you certainly won’t always get them, so don’t come to expect
them or try to force them.

---

When Breathing to Connect, allow yourself to feel whatever you’re feeling. Make room for those
feelings. You don’t have to like them; just let them be.

---

What’s The Role Of The Thinking Self In All This?

---

So far, in learning about connection we’ve focused on the observing self; on paying attention with
openness, receptiveness and interest. And we’ve tended to view the thinking self as a hindrance; as
something that disrupts our connection by distracting us with stories. But the thinking self can also
be of tremendous help to us— if we use it wisely. And that’s what the next chapter is all about.

---

Do any of the following thoughts sound familiar? “You’re not doing it right. You’re screwing it
up!’, ‘It’s useless. You may as well just give up now’, ‘This is so boring!’, ‘This is a complete
waste of time!’, ‘You blithering idiot! Why aren’t you practising what you read in that book?’,
“You dumb so-and-so! You completely forgot to try out those new techniques!’

---

As you work through this book, your thinking self will undoubtedly give you plenty of tonguelashings like these. But remember, it’s not deliberately trying to upset you—it’s just doing the job
that it evolved to do.

---

The observing self, as you know, doesn’t make judgements. It’s like a camera filming a wildlife
documentary. When the lion kills the antelope, the camera doesn’t judge it as good or bad; it simply
records what happens.
generation_rules: Practice acceptance techniques especially when caught up in thoughts and feelings
Do not use acceptance as a control strategy to feel good
Allow feelings to be present without needing to like them
Recognize the thinking self’s critical thoughts as natural and not deliberate harm
pause_rules: Pause to allow feelings to be noticed and made room for during breathing exercises
original_extraction.psychological_function: Encourages openness and receptiveness to present-moment experience; helps differentiate between the observing self and the thinking self; reduces self-critical thoughts by recognizing their evolutionary purpose.
repetition_rules: Repeatedly remind not to expect or force pleasant feelings from breathing exercises
symbolic_elements: observing self as a camera filming a wildlife documentary
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Facilitates acceptance of thoughts and feelings without judgment; reduces struggle with internal experiences; promotes mindful awareness through breathing exercises.
voice_rules: Normalize self-critical thoughts as evolutionary functions
